rules.title: Authentication Bypass via UserDefaults Flag
rules.description: The app uses a boolean from NSUserDefaults to determine authentication state, which can be trivially manipulated, allowing unauthorized access to the authenticated interface.
rules.remediation: Store authentication tokens in the iOS Keychain with kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly, and validate sessions server-side. Do not rely on mutable local storage for security decisions.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Install the app on a jailbroken device or use an iOS backup editor (e.g., iMazing).
2. Locate the app's preferences plist and set the key 'userLoggedIn' to boolean true.
3. Launch the app; it will skip the signup flow and present the main authenticated interface.

rules.title: Force-unwrap of nil NSString causes app crash
rules.description: The method unconditionally bridges a possibly nil Objective-C NSString to Swift String without nil check, leading to a crash if the text field returns nil.
rules.remediation: Check the returned NSString for nil before bridging, using `String(describing:)` or optional binding to safely handle nil values.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Tap submit button with empty username/password fields.
2. The app fetches the text property which may be nil if no text set.
3. Force unwrap causes a nil pointer exception and app crash.

rules.title: Core Data save error logs entire userInfo dictionary
rules.description: When a Core Data save fails, the error's userInfo dictionary is interpolated into an assertion message, potentially exposing sensitive data like database paths or user information in logs.
rules.remediation: Avoid logging raw userInfo; either sanitize the error details or omit them from production logging.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Trigger a Core Data save failure (e.g., fill storage or corrupt the store).
2. Examine console logs or crash reports.
3. Observe the logged assertion message containing NSError userInfo with sensitive details.

rules.title: Hardcoded encrypted secret and decryption routine exposes sensitive data
rules.description: The app embeds a hardcoded encrypted string and a custom decryption algorithm that produces a secret value, later inserted into an HTTP header. Attackers can reverse the binary to extract the secret.
rules.remediation: Never embed secrets in the client binary. Use server-side authentication and deliver secrets securely over the network.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Extract the app binary
2. Recover the hardcoded strings "abcde" and "dbbeddadbccbdaebaebdcbe" and the integer array
3. Reproduce the decryption algorithm to obtain the secret value

rules.title: Sensitive URL logged via print statements
rules.description: The loadPage method prints the full URL string three times to the console using Swift._print before loading it in a webview, potentially exposing sensitive information like tokens or PII in logs.
rules.remediation: Remove or disable the print statements in production builds; use os_log with privacy annotations to avoid logging sensitive data.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Obtain access to application logs.
2. Look for printed URLs with sensitive data.

rules.title: Sensitive error information logged via print statement
rules.description: Error descriptions and HTTP status codes are printed using `Swift::_print`, exposing potentially sensitive data in production logs.
rules.remediation: Remove print statements in release builds or use a logging framework with proper log level controls to suppress verbose output.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Trigger a network error (e.g., server error or invalid URL).
2. Observe logs via device console or Xcode.
3. Sensitive error details like localized descriptions appear in logs.

rules.title: Invalid UIViewController pointer (0x1) leads to crash
rules.description: The function initializes a sender variable with a hardcoded invalid pointer (0x1) and passes it to _showToast, causing a denial-of-service crash when the method attempts to use the object.
rules.remediation: Replace the hardcoded pointer with a valid UIViewController instance or remove the erroneous showToast call.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Trigger the signup network request (e.g., by tapping signup)
2. Wait for the request to complete
3. The app crashes when _showToast is called with invalid sender pointer

rules.title: Missing error check in response handler allows unauthorized login state
rules.description: The completion handler processes the response data and sets the userLoggedIn flag without checking if the Error parameter is nil, potentially marking the user as logged in even when the network request failed or returned an error.
rules.remediation: Check if the error parameter is nil and verify the HTTP status code indicates success before saving the JWT token and setting the userLoggedIn flag.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Initiate a network registration request that results in a failure (e.g., invalid server response, network timeout).
2. Observe that the completion handler is called with a non-nil Error parameter.
3. Notice the app still calls saveJWTToken and sets userLoggedIn to true, granting authenticated access without a valid token.

rules.title: Sensitive NSError userInfo logged via assertionFailure
rules.description: The closure interpolates the entire contents of an NSError's userInfo dictionary into a string and passes it to Swift._assertionFailure, potentially logging sensitive information (e.g., credentials, tokens) to console output.
rules.remediation: Avoid including the full userInfo dictionary in log messages; only log non-sensitive error details or use a redacted version.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Trigger an error in persistent store loading that contains sensitive data in the userInfo dictionary (e.g., authentication token).
2. Observe the application's console/log output.
3. The sensitive data is printed as part of the error description.

rules.title: Sensitive Error Information Logged to Console
rules.description: The application logs error descriptions to the console, which may contain sensitive information from network responses or user data, exposing it in device logs.
rules.remediation: Use a logging library that sanitizes logs or disable debug logging in production; log only error codes, not full description.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Trigger a network error that contains sensitive data (e.g., invalid login).
2. Observe that the error message is printed to the console.
3. Access device logs via Xcode to retrieve potentially sensitive information.

rules.title: Unvalidated pointer dereference with fixed offsets
rules.description: The function dereferences pointer param_1 at fixed offsets (8 and 24 bytes) without verifying the pointed-to buffer has sufficient size, risking out-of-bounds read and crash or information leak.
rules.remediation: Validate that the pointer points to a memory region of at least the required size before indexing with fixed offsets.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Craft a pointer pointing to a buffer smaller than 25 bytes
2. Call the function with param_2 = -1
3. The function will read beyond the buffer bounds, potentially crashing or leaking memory

rules.title: Use of uninitialized pointer in task_wait_throwing_resume_adapter
rules.description: The function calls a function pointer obtained from an uninitialized register (`unaff_x22`), potentially leading to arbitrary code execution if an attacker can control the register's value at call time.
rules.remediation: Ensure the function retrieves the function pointer from a validated parameter (e.g., `param_1`) instead of relying on an uninitialized register. Initialize or remove the invalid dereference.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Identify the calling context where x22 is set before entering this function.
2. If attacker can influence the value in x22, they can redirect execution to arbitrary code.
3. Exploit via memory corruption or input manipulation to set x22 to attacker-controlled address.

rules.title: Unvalidated Pointer Dereference in waitForStatusRecordUnlock
rules.description: The function reads a pointer from a status record at offset 0x50 and uses it without validation to perform a read-modify-write on offset -0x10, enabling an attacker who controls the record to write to arbitrary memory and corrupt a reference counter or adjacent data.
rules.remediation: Validate the pointer read from the status record before using it for reference count operations; consider null checking, address range validation, or using a trusted reference-counted wrapper.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Identify a caller-supplied AsyncTask pointer whose status record can be controlled.
2. Overwrite the field at +0x50 with a target address minus 0x10.
3. Trigger waitForStatusRecordUnlock to increment the value at that address, achieving an arbitrary write primitive.

rules.title: Out-of-bounds read in get_logo via unsafe pointer cast
rules.description: The function casts a raw string pointer to a String pointer and then accesses pSVar2[1].str without bounds checking, reading memory beyond the intended String object. This can leak adjacent heap data or cause a denial-of-service.
rules.remediation: Replace the unsafe pointer casting and manual indexing with safe Swift String accessors (e.g., use the `name` property directly) to avoid memory corruption.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Create an ImageResource object with a crafted name.
2. Call get_logo() on that object.
3. Observe potential crash or leak of sensitive data due to out-of-bounds memory access.

rules.title: Path traversal via unsanitized file parameter in GCDWebServerFileResponse init
rules.description: The init method passes the user-supplied file parameter directly to initWithFile:isAttachment: without any path sanitization, allowing directory traversal attacks if the file path is attacker-controllable.
rules.remediation: Validate the file path using stringByResolvingSymlinksInPath and ensure it remains within the intended base directory, or reject paths containing '..' components.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Identify an HTTP endpoint that creates a GCDWebServerFileResponse with a file path derived from user input.
2. Supply a crafted path such as '../../../etc/passwd'.
3. The server will read and return the arbitrary file.

rules.title: Unsanitized request path leads to arbitrary file read via NSBundle URLForResource
rules.description: The GCDWebServer request path is concatenated directly with "build" and used as a resource name in NSBundle URLForResource:withExtension: without sanitization, allowing an attacker to traverse directories and read arbitrary files from the application bundle or sandbox.
rules.remediation: Sanitize the request path by removing ".." components, resolving symlinks, and restricting the final path to stay within the intended resource directory. Alternatively, map allowed resource names without using path concatenation.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Connect to the GCDWebServer (e.g., http://<iphone-ip>:<port>)
2. Send a request with a crafted path like /../../../../Library/Preferences/com.apple.security.plist
3. The server will respond with the contents of the arbitrary file, e.g., sensitive preferences.

rules.title: Invalid pointer returned from _malloc wrapper (size not passed to allocator)
rules.description: The _malloc function calls an external allocation routine with no arguments and returns the input size_t value cast to a void pointer, creating an invalid pointer that will cause crashes or memory corruption when dereferenced.
rules.remediation: Pass the size parameter to the actual allocation function (e.g., PTR__malloc_100018178(param_1)) and return the result instead of the input.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call _malloc(0x1000)
2. Use the returned pointer (0x1000) to write data
3. Observe SIGSEGV because address 0x1000 is not mapped

rules.title: Null pointer dereference on AsyncContext parameter without prior validation
rules.description: The function directly dereferences param_2 to access memory at fixed offsets (e.g., +0x20) without any null-check, leading to a crash if param_2 is NULL.
rules.remediation: Add a null-check for param_2 before any dereference, or ensure callers always provide a valid pointer.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Invoke Swift concurrency waiting mechanism with a crafted or NULL AsyncContext.
2. The runtime enters this function.
3. The dereference occurs, crashing the process.

rules.title: Unchecked NULL pointer from pthread_getspecific may cause crash
rules.description: The return value of _pthread_getspecific is not validated for NULL before being offset and dereferenced, potentially leading to a crash.
rules.remediation: Check if the pointer returned by _pthread_getspecific is NULL before using it.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Trigger a scenario where the TLS value for key 0x68 is not set
2. Call adoptTaskVoucher
3. Application crashes

rules.title: Token stored to Keychain without kSecAttrAccessible
rules.description: The function persists an authentication token in the iOS Keychain but does not set the kSecAttrAccessible attribute. This may cause the token to be synced to iCloud Keychain and exposed across multiple devices.
rules.remediation: Add the key `kSecAttrAccessible` with value `kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly` to the Keychain query dictionary to prevent the token from being synchronized to iCloud.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Install the application on a device and log in to save the token.
2. Enable iCloud Keychain syncing.
3. Restore or log in on a second device; the token becomes accessible without user re-authentication.

rules.title: Type confusion: char pointer cast to NSObject* leads to invalid retain/release
rules.description: The equality function casts a field of a Swift String that likely contains a character pointer (char *) to NSObject* and subsequently calls _objc_retain and _objc_release on it. If that field holds a native char pointer rather than a valid ObjC object, this results in memory corruption or a crash.
rules.remediation: Access the correct union member (e.g., the bridged object pointer) when performing retain/release operations. Ensure a discriminator is checked before treating the data as an ObjC object.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Instantiate two FreshCart.ImageResource instances where the 'name' property contains a string that is stored as a native small string (non-bridged)
2. Invoke the '==' operator on them (e.g., via comparison)
3. Observe app crash or undefined memory behavior when _objc_retain operates on a non-NSObject pointer

rules.title: Core Data save error details including userInfo logged via assertion failure
rules.description: When a Core Data save fails, the error's userInfo dictionary (which may contain sensitive model data) is interpolated into a string passed to _assertionFailure, potentially leaking data to logs/crash reports.
rules.remediation: Avoid logging raw error details. Use a generic failure message and ensure sensitive information is not included in logs, especially in production builds.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Cause a Core Data save error (e.g. unique constraint violation).
2. Observe the crash log or console output containing "Unresolved error" followed by the error's userInfo dictionary with sensitive data.

rules.title: Insecure PKCS7 padding removal may enable padding oracle attack
rules.description: The function calls Padding::_remove without constant-time verification or uniform error handling, likely leaking timing information that could allow an attacker to perform a padding oracle attack.
rules.remediation: Replace Padding::_remove with a constant-time padding removal function that does not leak success/failure through timing or control flow. Ensure uniform error handling for all padding errors.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Intercept encrypted data with PKCS7 padding.
2. Modify the last ciphertext block and send to the decryption endpoint.
3. Measure processing time or observe error differences to distinguish valid from invalid padding.
4. Recover plaintext byte-by-byte.

rules.title: Use of Weak Cryptographic Hash (MD5)
rules.description: The method computes an MD5 hash, which is cryptographically broken and susceptible to collision attacks; should not be used for security-sensitive operations.
rules.remediation: Replace MD5 with a secure hash function such as SHA-256 or SHA-512.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Pass any string to the md5 method
2. The hash output is generated using MD5
3. MD5 collisions can be exploited to forge data or bypass integrity checks

rules.title: Use of Weak SHA1 Hashing Algorithm
rules.description: The function computes an SHA1 hash, which is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to collision attacks. This can undermine integrity checks or password security.
rules.remediation: Replace SHA1 with a secure algorithm such as SHA256 or SHA512.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Invoke sha1() on a string
2. Rely on the hash for integrity verification or password storage
3. Exploit known SHA1 collisions to forge data or compromise accounts

rules.title: Timing side-channel in CMAC subkey generation due to secret-dependent branch
rules.description: The function performs a conditional XOR with the Rb constant during subkey derivation based on the most significant bit of a key-dependent byte. This branching is not constant-time and may leak key material via timing differences.
rules.remediation: Implement the conditional XOR using constant-time operations, such as mask generation with arithmetic shifts and bitwise operations, to eliminate the data-dependent branch.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Supply known messages to the CMAC authenticate function and measure execution time for each.
2. Observe timing variations correlated with the MSB of the computed subkey bytes.
3. Collect enough samples to infer key bits using statistical analysis.

rules.title: RSA PKCS1v1.5 padding uses all-zero bytes instead of random non-zero bytes
rules.description: The RSA encryption prepare function for variant 1 fills the padding with zero bytes, violating PKCS#1 v1.5 specification that requires at least 8 random non-zero bytes. This makes the RSA encryption deterministic and vulnerable to chosen-ciphertext attacks.
rules.remediation: Generate padding bytes from a cryptographically secure random number generator (non-zero) and include the correct PKCS#1 v1.5 block format (0x00 || 0x02 || random bytes || 0x00 || data) or switch to OAEP padding.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call the prepare function with variant=1 and a plaintext.
2. Encrypt the plaintext multiple times; observe identical ciphertext outputs (no randomness).
3. Exploit determinism to decrypt intercepted ciphertexts or forge signatures.

rules.title: Double release of plaintext bridge object in RSA.encrypt
rules.description: The function releases the plaintext Swift bridge object twice via _swift_bridgeObjectRelease, leading to a double free / reference count underflow and potential use-after-free.
rules.remediation: Remove the redundant _swift_bridgeObjectRelease(param_2) call; rely on ARC or ensure exactly one release.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Create an RSA instance with a key.
2. Call encrypt with arbitrary plaintext bytes.
3. On success, the plaintext object's reference count is decremented twice, risking memory corruption.

rules.title: RSA decryption without padding verification (textbook RSA)
rules.description: The function performs raw RSA modular exponentiation on the input ciphertext without any padding verification, exposing the decryption to malleability and adaptive chosen-ciphertext attacks.
rules.remediation: Apply OAEP (Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding) and validate the padding structure after the modular exponentiation before returning the plaintext.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Intercept an RSA ciphertext
2. Multiply the ciphertext by r^e mod n for a known r
3. Submit the modified ciphertext for decryption and derive plaintext from the result via malleability

rules.title: Heap buffer overflow due to out-of-bounds array write in publicKeyDER
rules.description: The array is allocated with size 2, but subsequent code writes to indices 3 and 4, causing a heap overflow that may lead to arbitrary code execution.
rules.remediation: Increase the array allocation count to match the actual number of stored elements (e.g., 5) and ensure all indices are within bounds.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Create an RSA instance with a maliciously crafted key.
2. Invoke the publicKeyDER method.
3. Heap corruption occurs, potentially enabling code execution.

rules.title: Uninitialized stack variable passed to swift_getWitnessTable
rules.description: The function declares local_20 as undefined8 but does not initialize it before passing it as the third argument to _swift_getWitnessTable. The callee may interpret the stale stack value as a pointer, leading to potential crash or information disclosure.
rules.remediation: Initialize local_20 to a safe value (e.g., 0 or NULL) before the call, or modify the runtime to accept fewer arguments if not needed.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Trigger a Swift range expression using PartialRangeUpTo<Int> that causes this witness table accessor to run for the first time.
2. Observe potential crash due to dereferencing a stale stack pointer.
3. Alternatively, inspect stack contents before the call to detect information leak.

rules.title: Unvalidated index leads to potential arbitrary code execution in function dispatcher
rules.description: The function calculateHash uses param_2 as an index into a jump table without bounds checking, allowing an out-of-bounds read of a function pointer that can lead to arbitrary code execution if param_2 is attacker-controlled.
rules.remediation: Add a bounds check to ensure param_2 is within the valid range of the jump table, or use a safe dispatch mechanism like a switch statement.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Identify attacker-controlled input that influences param_2.
2. Provide index value that exceeds table size to read arbitrary memory.
3. Craft target address to redirect execution when function pointer is called.

rules.title: RSA Signature Padding Bypass via Conditional Flag
rules.description: The pad function uses a boolean flag (param_3) to conditionally skip RSA padding, allowing an attacker to force raw or unpadded signatures that are trivially forgeable.
rules.remediation: Always apply a secure padding scheme and remove the condition that disables padding. Additionally, replace the hardcoded padding type constant (5) with a defined, secure standard.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Invoke the pad function with param_3 set to 0 (false).
2. Observe that no padding is applied and the raw message is returned.
3. Use the raw, unpadded data in an RSA signature context to bypass integrity checks.

rules.title: Missing array bounds check in jump table allows arbitrary code execution
rules.description: The function indexes a global function pointer table using `param_2.value` cast to byte without any bounds validation. An attacker controlling `param_2.value` can cause an out-of-bounds read, leading to a call to an arbitrary address.
rules.remediation: Validate that `param_2.value` is within the allocated jump table bounds before using it as an index, or re-implement as a bound-checked switch statement.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Attacker supplies a crafted SignatureVariant with a `value` outside the valid range (0-? unknown).
2. The table index over-reads into attacker-controlled memory.
3. The function pointer dereference and call execute attacker-chosen code.

rules.title: Potential double free of closure context in resume handler
rules.description: The resume function unconditionally frees the context pointer pvVar2 at the end, regardless of whether the context has already been freed. If the continuation is resumed multiple times, this leads to a double-free vulnerability.
rules.remediation: Ensure the context is freed only once, e.g., by setting the pointer to null after freeing and checking before freeing again, or by guaranteeing the continuation is resumed exactly once.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Trigger the async operation that calls this resume handler.
2. Cause the operation to be resumed multiple times (e.g., race condition, cancellation error).
3. The second invocation will call _free on the already-freed pointer, corrupting the heap.

rules.title: Hardcoded flag string in plaintext
rules.description: The application sets a UILabel's text to a hardcoded string "Flag 'ere!", which is the target flag for the CTF challenge but represents a hardcoded secret that can be trivially extracted via static analysis.
rules.remediation: Do not hardcode secrets; deliver the flag dynamically from a server or use obfuscation if the flag must be embedded.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Decompile the binary using Ghidra or similar.
2. Search for the string "Flag 'ere!" or the Swift.String.init call.
3. Retrieve the flag value.

rules.title: Missing IV length validation in CFB initializer
rules.description: The CFB initializer stores the provided IV array directly without validating that its length equals the block size of the underlying cipher (e.g., 16 bytes for AES). This can lead to runtime errors or incorrect cryptographic operations.
rules.remediation: Add an explicit length check in the initializer that compares the IV count with the block size, and throws a Swift error or asserts if they do not match.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Import CryptoSwift in a Swift project.
2. Create a CFB instance with an IV array of invalid length (e.g., 1 byte).
3. Use the instance for encryption/decryption.
4. The operation may crash or produce wrong ciphertext.

rules.title: Missing negative check on blockSize parameter allows integer underflow
rules.description: The function only checks if blockSize equals zero but does not verify it is positive. A negative blockSize can be supplied, causing integer underflow, large allocation, and potential memory corruption.
rules.remediation: Explicitly validate that blockSize > 0 and allowance >= 0 at the entry of the function.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call bitPadding with a negative blockSize (e.g., -1) and any allowance.
2. Observe that the zero-check on blockSize is bypassed.
3. The subsequent arithmetic leads to a huge count passed to Array.init, causing a crash or memory exhaustion.

rules.title: AES S-Box lookup not constant-time (potential cache-timing side-channel)
rules.description: The S-Box table lookup in the AES SubWord operation uses a secret-dependent array index, making it susceptible to cache-timing side-channel attacks that can recover the encryption key.
rules.remediation: Implement a constant-time lookup technique such as using a masked S-Box or bit-slicing to avoid data-dependent memory accesses.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Run a process co-located with the target app.
2. Perform Prime+Probe cache timing on the S-Box table memory.
3. Measure access times for each S-Box entry during AES key expansion.
4. Use statistical analysis to recover the secret key bytes.

rules.title: Use of uninitialized register in pointer arithmetic leading to arbitrary read
rules.description: The function reads a 64-bit value from an address formed by adding an integer read from an offset within param_1's size field to the uninitialized register unaff_x20. This can lead to arbitrary memory disclosure or crash.
rules.remediation: Initialize the base pointer (likely 'this') properly and validate that the index derived from size stays within the object's memory bounds.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Obtain a BatchedCollection instance with a controlled size field.
2. Ensure the value at (param_1.size + 0x24) is attacker-controlled.
3. Trigger get_size after a prior operation that leaves a known pointer in unaff_x20.
4. The returned value leaks data at an attacker-chosen offset.

rules.title: ChaChaEncryptor.update skips encryption of final partial block on isLast=true
rules.description: The update method ignores the isLast flag and fails to encrypt remaining bytes when the input size is not a multiple of 64, leaking plaintext in the final partial block.
rules.remediation: When isLast is true, after processing full blocks, encrypt any remaining bytes using the final approach (e.g., pad/truncate) and append to output.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Instantiate ChaCha20 encryptor with key and nonce
2. Call update with 65 bytes and isLast=false -> returns 64 ciphertext bytes, 1 byte remains in state
3. Call update with empty input and isLast=true -> no additional ciphertext returned; final byte never encrypted and lost

rules.title: Out-of-bounds read/write in BigUInt.add due to missing destination size check
rules.description: The add function uses shiftedBy + local_60 as an index into the destination BigUInt without verifying that the index is within the destination's bounds, allowing out-of-bounds read and write when shiftedBy is too large or the destination is too small.
rules.remediation: Add a bounds check to ensure that (shiftedBy + local_60) < destination.count before calling get_subscript or set_subscript on the destination.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Create a BigUInt with a small internal buffer (e.g., capacity 1).
2. Call add() with parameter shiftedBy set to a large value (e.g., 1000).
3. The function will access out-of-bounds memory, potentially corrupting adjacent heap data.

rules.title: Unvalidated string input causes crash via assertionFailure in BigUInt init
rules.description: The BigUInt initializer from a string literal does not validate the format and invokes Swift._assertionFailure on malformed input, causing a denial of service through an unhandled crash.
rules.remediation: Validate the input string format or use a failable/throwing initializer instead of assertionFailure to allow graceful error handling.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Provide an invalid numeric string (e.g. 'abc') to BigUInt(stringLiteral:)
2. Initiate the conversion
3. The application crashes due to the assertion failure

rules.title: Potential Denial of Service via Integer Overflow Trap in BigUInt.extract
rules.description: The function performs unchecked integer arithmetic that can overflow, leading to a software breakpoint (trap) and crash, enabling denial-of-service when malicious range values are supplied.
rules.remediation: Use overflow-safe operators (&+, &-) or validate inputs to ensure arithmetic cannot overflow.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call BigUInt.extract with a Range where the lower bound is large enough that adding a computed offset overflows Int64.
2. Observe the application crash due to the software breakpoint.

rules.title: Non-constant-time BigUInt comparison leaks timing information
rules.description: The compare function performs an early-exit loop over big integer words, returning as soon as a difference is found. Timing varies with the position of the first differing digit, enabling side-channel attacks on secret keys.
rules.remediation: Use a constant-time comparison that accumulates a flag for all word differences without early exit, for example: result |= (unsigned)(a[i] - b[i]); return (result != 0).
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Provide two large BigUInt values that differ at a known word index.
2. Measure the execution time of compare().
3. Correlate timing differences to leak the word index of the first difference.

rules.title: BigUInt serialize lacks maximum bitWidth check, allowing allocation-based DoS
rules.description: The serialize function allocates memory based on the BigUInt's bitWidth without enforcing an upper bound. An attacker can supply a crafted BigUInt with a huge bitWidth to cause an out-of-memory crash.
rules.remediation: Add an explicit maximum allowed bitWidth (e.g., 4 KB or another application-appropriate limit) before computing the byte size, and reject the operation if exceeded.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Construct a BigUInt object with a very large bitWidth (e.g., 2^60)
2. Invoke the serialize() method on it
3. Observe the app attempt to allocate gigabytes of memory and crash

rules.title: Data-dependent branch in division remainder may enable timing side-channel attack
rules.description: The formRemainder function uses a conditional branch (add/subtract vs subtract only) based on the result of a big-integer comparison, which can leak secret key material through timing differences.
rules.remediation: Refactor the division to use constant-time operations (e.g., bitwise conditional moves) instead of data-dependent branches, ensuring uniform execution time regardless of input values.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Perform repeated remainder operations with attacker-controlled dividend and known divisor while measuring CPU time.
2. Observe timing variations correlated with the secret-dependent branch.
3. Apply statistical analysis to infer secret bits (e.g., private key material).

rules.title: Missing division-by-zero check in BigUInt infix operator
rules.description: The function __infix calls quotientAndRemainder without verifying that the divisor is non-zero, which may cause a runtime trap and application termination, leading to denial of service.
rules.remediation: Add a guard statement to check for a zero divisor and throw a custom error or return a safe value instead of allowing the trap.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Invoke the infix operator with a zero divisor.
2. Observe the application crash due to an unhandled exception.

rules.title: Potential Pointer Truncation in BigUInt Division Leading to Out-of-Bounds Access
rules.description: A storage pointer is cast to a byte, truncating the address, and then used to construct a BigUInt operand for a divide operation, risking memory corruption.
rules.remediation: Ensure pointer-to-integer casts preserve full pointer width; use Swift's unsafe pointer APIs without truncation or avoid manual casts.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Create a BigUInt divisor with a storage pointer whose upper bytes are non-zero
2. Invoke the /= operator on a BigUInt with this divisor
3. The divide function will operate on a truncated address, potentially causing an out-of-bounds read/write or crash.

rules.title: Modulus divisor truncated to single byte in BigUInt %= infix operator
rules.description: The divisor parameter (param_3) is cast to a single byte before being used in the modulus operation, effectively reducing the modulus to values 0-255. This completely breaks cryptographic operations relying on large integer arithmetic (RSA, DSA, etc.) and allows trivial recovery of secrets.
rules.remediation: Ensure the divisor is used as a full-precision BigUInt. Remove the erroneous byte cast and correctly pass the entire big integer storage to formRemainder.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Use any cryptographic function that invokes the BigUInt %= operator (e.g., modular exponentiation in RSA).
2. Observe that the modulus operation is performed with a divisor truncated to 8 bits.
3. Demonstrate that the remainder is computed modulo a value between 0 and 255, leading to immediate key recovery or data leakage.

rules.title: Modular exponentiation not constant-time, leaks exponent via timing
rules.description: The modular exponentiation iterates over exponent bits and conditionally executes a multiplication and modulus reduction when a bit is set. This timing side-channel can expose the secret exponent.
rules.remediation: Replace the branching square-and-multiply with a constant-time algorithm such as Montgomery ladder or always perform dummy multiplications.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call the power function with a known base, modulus, and secret exponent.
2. Measure execution time with high-precision timer.
3. Repeat multiple times and correlate time spikes with exponent bits to recover the key.

rules.title: Missing validation on direct multiplication limit
rules.description: The setter for directMultiplicationLimit accepts an unrestricted integer value without validation. An attacker controlling this value could set a maliciously large or negative threshold, causing unsafe arithmetic behavior, denial of service, or side-channel information leaks in cryptographic multiplication.
rules.remediation: Add input validation to ensure the limit is within a safe range (e.g., 1 to 4096 bits) before assignment.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call set_directMultiplicationLimit(-1) or set_directMultiplicationLimit(0x7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF)
2. Invoke any BigUInt multiplication operation
3. Observe excessive memory consumption or algorithm downgrade

rules.title: Reachable assertion leads to crash on invalid input
rules.description: The function uses `_assertionFailure` for precondition checks (input > 1 and witness > 0) instead of returning false, causing a crash if an attacker can supply zero or one values.
rules.remediation: Replace `_assertionFailure` with a return of false for invalid inputs, to avoid crashing the application.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call isStrongProbablePrime with param_1 set to 0 or 1
2. Observe the application crashes due to assertion failure

rules.title: Primality test always returns true, bypassing all validation
rules.description: The _isPrime function unconditionally returns true, never testing the input for primality. This allows composite numbers to be accepted as prime, completely undermining cryptographic key generation and other security-critical operations that rely on this check.
rules.remediation: Implement a correct probabilistic primality test (e.g., Miller-Rabin) using the provided rounds parameter, or ensure the function dispatches to a proper testing routine.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call _isPrime with any composite number (e.g., 4).
2. Observe it returns true, which would indicate 4 is prime.

rules.title: Unvalidated shift amount `shiftedBy` may cause out-of-bounds memory access
rules.description: The `shiftedBy` parameter is passed directly to a low-level C function without validation, which could be used as a shift or index. A negative or excessively large value may lead to out-of-bounds read/write or undefined behavior, compromising memory safety.
rules.remediation: Validate `shiftedBy` to be non-negative and within a safe range (e.g., 0 to wordSize * arrayLength-1) before passing it to the underlying C function.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Invoke `subtractingWord` with a negative `shiftedBy` (e.g., -1) or a value exceeding the internal buffer size.
2. The call propagates to `subtractWord`, which may use it as a shift amount or index without bounds checking.
3. Undefined behavior results, potentially corrupting memory or allowing controlled out-of-bounds access.

rules.title: Unvalidated negative shift causes assertion failure (crash)
rules.description: The function does not validate that the `shiftedBy` parameter is non-negative before triggering a Swift `assertionFailure`, which results in an unrecoverable crash if a negative value is supplied.
rules.remediation: Validate that `shiftedBy >= 0` before proceeding, or replace the precondition with a recoverable error mechanism (e.g., throwing an error or returning an invalid state).
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call subtractReportingOverflow with shiftedBy = -1
2. Function triggers precondition failure
3. Application crashes

rules.title: Denial of Service via Unvalidated BigUInt Subtraction Overflow
rules.description: The function performs BigUInt subtraction without ensuring the subtrahend is not larger than the minuend. Overflow triggers a Swift assertion failure, crashing the app if an attacker supplies crafted inputs.
rules.remediation: Validate that the subtrahend is less than or equal to the minuend before subtraction, or handle the overflow gracefully (e.g., return nil or throw) instead of trapping.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Provide BigUInt instance 'a' = 5
2. Provide BigUInt instance 'b' = 10
3. Call subtract(a, 0, b)
4. Observe application crash from assertion failure

rules.title: Unvalidated 'shiftedBy' parameter may cause out-of-bounds memory access
rules.description: The 'shiftedBy' integer parameter is passed directly to the internal 'subtract' function without any validation, potentially allowing an attacker to supply a negative or excessively large shift value that leads to an out-of-bounds array access or integer overflow in the big-integer digit buffer.
rules.remediation: Add a check that 'shiftedBy' is non-negative and does not exceed the maximum digit count of the BigUInt operands before using it in the subtraction/shift logic.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call the 'subtracting' method with a shiftedBy value of -1 or a very large integer that exceeds the internal digit array length.
2. Observe memory corruption, crash, or unexpected behavior.

rules.title: Bit length truncated to 8 bits causing generation of small primes
rules.description: The generatePrime function casts the BigUInt bitLength parameter to a byte, discarding all but the least significant 8 bits. This can cause randomInteger to generate numbers with a drastically smaller width than intended (e.g., 256-bit input becomes 0 bits), leading to trivially factorable primes and broken cryptography.
rules.remediation: Remove the byte cast and pass the full BigUInt bitLength to randomInteger without truncation.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call generatePrime(256)
2. Observe that the returned prime has only 256 % 256 = 0 bits (tiny value such as 2 or 3)
3. Verify that RSA keys generated with such primes are instantly breakable

rules.title: ChaCha20 initializer ignores key and uses IV as key
rules.description: The ___allocating_init call passes the IV bytes for both key and IV, completely ignoring the supplied key. This causes encryption to use the publicly visible IV as key, enabling trivial decryption.
rules.remediation: Pass the correct key bytes as the second argument to ___allocating_init, not the IV bytes.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Capture encrypted communication.
2. Extract the IV from the message prefix.
3. Decrypt using the IV as the ChaCha20 key.

rules.title: ChaCha20.init accepts weak key lengths (8 or 12 bytes)
rules.description: The initializer allows key arrays of length 8 or 12 bytes, which is far below the required 32-byte (256-bit) key for ChaCha20. This drastically reduces cipher strength, enabling practical brute-force attacks.
rules.remediation: Enforce a minimum key length of 32 bytes (256 bits) by checking count == 32, and throw an error for any other length.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Create a ChaCha20 instance with a key array of 8 random bytes.
2. Encrypt a known plaintext.
3. Perform exhaustive 2^64 key search to recover the key.

rules.title: Unvalidated enum raw value used as jump table index in Equatable conformance
rules.description: The function dereferences a jump table using (byte)param_1.value as index without bounds checking. If an attacker can control the enum's raw value, this leads to an out-of-bounds read and call to an uncontrolled function pointer, likely resulting in arbitrary code execution.
rules.remediation: Validate raw values at the point of deserialization to ensure they map to a defined enum case. Use a failable initializer, guard statement, or exhaustive switch before creating instances. Never trust raw integer values to directly index function tables.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Locate any external interface (JSON deserialization, user defaults, URL scheme, etc.) that constructs a FailedCheck instance with a raw value derived from attacker input.
2. Provide a raw value outside the intended enum case range (e.g., 0xFF).
3. Trigger an equality check (e.g., by inserting the instance into a Set or using ==). The vulnerable function will execute, using the attacker-controlled byte as an index into the jump table, diverting control flow to an attacker-controlled address.

rules.title: Unchecked jump table index from user-controlled input
rules.description: The function uses param_2.value truncated to a byte as an index into a function pointer table without validating the index bounds, allowing an attacker to redirect execution to an unintended function or cause a crash.
rules.remediation: Validate that param_2.value is within the expected range of the dispatch table before indexing, or ensure a default safe handler is always present.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Identify entry point that supplies the FailedCheck structure to hash().
2. Set param_2.value to an arbitrary byte value outside the expected range.
3. Observe invocation of an unexpected handler function or application crash.

rules.title: Missing Minimum Padding Length Validation in EME-PKCS1v15
rules.description: The function computes padding length as 'local_48 = param_2 - lVar1' but never enforces the PKCS#1 v1.5 requirement that the padding string (PS) must be at least 8 bytes, which can lead to cryptographically weak ciphertexts vulnerable to Bleichenbacher attacks.
rules.remediation: Add an explicit check that local_48 >= 8 (or that the overall key size ensures the minimum padding) and raise an error or abort if the condition is violated.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call add() with an input array length such that (inputSize + 3) % blockSize equals blockSize - 3..blockSize - 7
2. Observe that local_48 (padding length) becomes less than 8
3. The generated padded message has insufficient random bytes, violating the spec

rules.title: Sensitive NSError userInfo logged during Core Data save failure
rules.description: On Core Data save failure, the error's userInfo dictionary is interpolated into a log string and passed to assertionFailure, potentially leaking sensitive data like file paths or model details in crash logs or console output.
rules.remediation: Sanitize the error message before logging; avoid including the raw NSError userInfo dictionary, or redact sensitive keys like NSSQLiteErrorDomain file paths.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Trigger a Core Data save failure (e.g., by modifying the data model without migration).
2. The error's userInfo is logged via assertionFailure, which may crash the app or output to console/crash logs.
3. Extract the log to obtain sensitive information embedded in the error's userInfo.

rules.title: Stack buffer overflow via unsafe memcpy in Words init
rules.description: The function copies 33 bytes (0x21) from param_1 into a local stack area starting at &local_58 that spans only 28 bytes (local_58..local_31), causing a 5-byte overflow onto adjacent stack data. This can lead to memory corruption and potential code execution if the source BigInt is attacker-controlled.
rules.remediation: Ensure the destination buffer is at least 33 bytes in size, or use a safe copy function that validates the destination capacity. Alternatively, declare the local buffer explicitly as a 33-byte array instead of relying on individual field layout.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Prepare a malicious BigInt object with crafted internal representation (33 bytes).
2. Invoke Words.init(_:) with that BigInt.
3. The memcpy overflows the stack buffer, overwriting adjacent variables and potentially the return address, leading to control flow hijack.

rules.title: Hardcoded true return in BigInt::get_isSigned ignores actual sign
rules.description: The get_isSigned method unconditionally returns true, disregarding the actual signedness of the BigInt instance. This can cause logic errors if callers rely on it for sign-dependent operations.
rules.remediation: Return the actual sign flag stored in the BigInt instance (e.g., access a member variable) instead of a hardcoded true.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Create a BigInt object with an unsigned internal representation.
2. Call get_isSigned() on that object.
3. Observe that the method returns true instead of false.
4. Any subsequent code that treats the number as signed may perform incorrect arithmetic or validation.

rules.title: Uncontrolled memory allocation in BigInt bitwise OR via unvalidated word count
rules.description: The function does not validate the maximum word count of the input BigInt objects before allocating an array of that size, allowing an attacker to trigger out-of-memory conditions and crash the application.
rules.remediation: Limit the maximum permissible word count (e.g., 1<<24) before calling reserveCapacity, and reject or truncate oversized BigInt inputs.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Construct a BigInt with a word count of e.g., 1<<30
2. Supply it as either operand to the bitwise OR operation
3. Observe massive memory allocation and application crash due to resource exhaustion

rules.title: Stack information disclosure via uninitialized memory copy in BigInt |= operator
rules.description: The function copies 33 bytes from an uninitialized stack buffer `auStack_38` into the `param_1` BigInt, potentially leaking sensitive stack data.
rules.remediation: Zero-initialize the stack buffer before use or avoid copying from uninitialized memory.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Invoke the BigInt `|=` operation with crafted input.
2. Access the resulting BigInt's internal buffer representation.
3. Read the leaked stack contents, which may include pointers or other sensitive data.

rules.title: Uninitialized stack read in BigInt division assignment operator
rules.description: The function copies 33 bytes from the uninitialised local buffer auStack_60 into the inout BigInt parameter, potentially leaking sensitive stack data (e.g., keys) into the DIV result.
rules.remediation: Ensure the result of the internal __infix call is stored into a valid local variable before copying, or zero-initialize auStack_60.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Create two BigInt objects (dividend and divisor).
2. Call dividend /= divisor.
3. Examine the resulting BigInt’s internal data – it will contain uninitialised stack content.

rules.title: Non-constant-time modular exponentiation leaks exponent bits via timing side-channel
rules.description: The modular exponentiation implementation branches on each bit of the exponent, performing different operations (e.g., multiply vs. skip). This creates observable timing discrepancies that can allow an attacker to recover secret exponent values.
rules.remediation: Replace the square-and-multiply loop with a constant-time exponentiation algorithm, such as Montgomery ladder, ensuring no data-dependent branches or memory accesses.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Attacker supplies a known modulus and base, and obtains ciphertext or signature with a secret exponent.
2. Attacker measures execution time of the power operation multiple times with the same inputs.
3. Timing differences reveal the exponent bits (e.g., longer time for bit=1 due to extra multiplication).

rules.title: Use of uninitialized pointer in get_hashValue
rules.description: The function copies 33 bytes from an uninitialized pointer (unaff_x20) into a stack buffer via _memcpy, potentially reading from an attacker-controlled or invalid memory address, leading to crash or information disclosure.
rules.remediation: Replace raw memcpy on an uninitialized pointer with a safe Swift hash of the struct's fields, or ensure the source pointer is properly initialized before use.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Instantiate a BigInt with crafted internal state\.
2. Call the hashValue getter\.
3. Observe crash or leakage of process memory from the uninitialized pointer\.

rules.title: Unvalidated shift amount in BigInt left shift leads to denial of service
rules.description: The function extracts a shift amount from the second operand without any bounds checking and passes it directly to shiftedLeft. A maliciously large value can cause excessive memory allocation and crash.
rules.remediation: Add a maximum shift width check before calling shiftedLeft, for example by comparing the shift amount to a predefined limit and returning an error or capping the shift.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Create a BigInt for the shift amount with a value like 2^32.
2. Call the << infix operator with this shift amount.
3. The library will try to allocate an enormous buffer, leading to memory exhaustion and application crash.

rules.title: Missing validation on left shift amount can lead to DoS via memory exhaustion
rules.description: The left shift operation does not limit the shift amount, allowing an attacker to trigger excessive memory allocation and crash the application via an out-of-memory condition.
rules.remediation: Validate the shift amount to ensure it does not exceed a safe maximum, such as the maximum bit length of the resulting BigInt to prevent excessive memory allocation.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Provide a large shift amount (e.g., 2^31-1) as the right operand to the BigInt left shift function.
2. Observe that the application crashes due to out-of-memory or memory pressure.
3. Repeat with various large values to confirm no upper bound.

rules.title: Uninitialized stack buffer used as source in memcpy leading to information leak
rules.description: The function copies uninitialized stack memory (auStack_60) into the output parameter, which can leak sensitive data from the stack including potential cryptographic keys or secrets.
rules.remediation: Ensure the destination buffer is initialized with zeroes or a proper computed result before writing; fix the logic to copy the correct result (likely from auStack_38).
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Call the subtraction function with any BigInt values.
2. The resulting BigInt will contain uninitialized stack data that may include cryptographic keys or other secrets.
3. Inspect the result to extract leaked data.

rules.title: Leftover Debug Breakpoint in BigInt bitWidth Calculation
rules.description: The overflow handler uses SoftwareBreakpoint, which will crash the app if ever triggered. This debug code should not exist in production builds.
rules.remediation: Replace with a proper overflow guard (e.g., preconditionFailure) that is removed in release builds, or use Swift's overflow operators.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Construct a BigInt whose bit width addition overflows when incremented by 1
2. Invoke get_bitWidth, causing the SoftwareBreakpoint to trigger and crash the app

rules.title: Weak Block Cipher Blowfish in CBC Mode Initialization
rules.description: The function initializes Blowfish block cipher in CBC mode. Blowfish has a 64‑bit block size, making it susceptible to birthday attacks (Sweet32) after encrypting a large volume of data, potentially leading to plaintext recovery.
rules.remediation: Replace Blowfish with a modern cipher that uses at least a 128-bit block size, such as AES‑GCM or AES‑CBC with proper IV handling.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Identify that the application uses Blowfish/CBC encryption.
2. Capture several gigabytes of ciphertext (e.g., 2–4 GB) through repeated sessions or a long-lived stream.
3. Exploit the Sweet32 attack to recover plaintext from the captured traffic.

rules.title: Simple XOR cipher used for flag encryption
rules.description: The closure performs a bytewise XOR with a static key, a weak obfuscation method that does not provide confidentiality or authenticity.
rules.remediation: Replace XOR with a standard authenticated encryption algorithm such as AES-GCM and securely manage keys.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Capture the XOR-ed data (likely the flag string).
2. Identify the static key byte(s) used (hardcoded or derived from a constant).
3. Apply XOR with the known key to recover the plaintext flag.

rules.title: Core Data persistent store created without file protection
rules.description: The NSPersistentContainer is initialized and persistent stores are loaded without specifying NSPersistentStoreFileProtectionKey, leaving the SQLite database file exposed to unauthorized access when the device is unlocked.
rules.remediation: Before calling loadPersistentStores, configure the persistentStoreDescriptions array with an NSPersistentStoreDescription that sets the NSPersistentStoreFileProtectionKey option to NSFileProtectionComplete.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Decompile the app binary.
2. Observe the NSPersistentContainer getter creates the container with only a name, then immediately calls loadPersistentStoresWithCompletionHandler.
3. Note the absence of NSPersistentStoreDescription configuration with NSPersistentStoreFileProtectionKey.
4. The resulting database file at the default path will lack system-level file protection, making it readable by any process/user when the device is unlocked.

rules.title: Sensitive error userInfo logged via assertionFailure
rules.description: The NSError userInfo dictionary is bridged and string-interpolated into an assertion failure message, potentially exposing sensitive data in crash logs.
rules.remediation: Avoid logging the entire userInfo dictionary; use a generic error description or sanitize the dictionary before logging.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Trigger a persistent store load failure with user-controlled userInfo (e.g., via a tampered Core Data store).
2. Inspect device crash logs or Xcode console for the assertionFailure message containing sensitive data.

rules.title: Double release of Swift string parameter may cause memory corruption
rules.description: The function calls _swift_bridgeObjectRelease(param_2) twice on the same parameter, resulting in a double free that could lead to heap corruption or use-after-free.
rules.remediation: Ensure that the string parameter is released exactly once by removing the redundant _swift_bridgeObjectRelease call or fixing the ARC balance.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Invoke the initializer with a crafted Swift String parameter.
2. If the initial retain count is low, the first release frees the memory, and the second release operates on a dangling pointer, potentially causing a crash or exploitable heap corruption.

rules.title: Out-of-bounds read in tag decoder due to unchecked buffer size
rules.description: The function reads from the input buffer at offset 1 when param_2 > 0xf6 without verifying that the buffer is actually large enough, potentially leaking adjacent memory or crashing the application.
rules.remediation: Validate that the buffer pointed to by param_1 is at least as large as the required read offset (e.g., ensure the buffer length is greater than the computed `local_14`-byte field at offset 1).
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Craft a serialized payload with a param_2 value > 0xf6 but a truncated param_1 buffer (e.g., length 0).
2. Invoke the function with this payload.
3. Observe out-of-bounds read causing crash or memory leak.

rules.title: Potential out-of-bounds read in enum tag witness due to missing buffer size validation
rules.description: The function unconditionally reads from offsets inside the payload buffer (param_1) without validating the buffer size, relying on param_2 solely for control flow. An attacker who influences param_2 or the buffer could trigger an out-of-bounds read, potentially causing a denial-of-service or limited information disclosure.
rules.remediation: Add explicit bounds checking using a known buffer size parameter, or ensure that all callers always provide a buffer large enough for the maximum payload of the enum.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Craft an enum payload with a tag value (param_2) set to a negative number.
2. Provide a truncated or undersized buffer for param_1.
3. Invoke the witness function; the code accesses param_1[6] and *param_1 beyond the allocated memory.

rules.title: Uninitialized AES pointer passed to _encrypt
rules.description: Local variable `in_x4` is declared as `AES *` but never initialized before being passed to `CryptoSwift::AES::_encrypt()`, causing undefined behavior, potential crash, or arbitrary code execution.
rules.remediation: Initialize `in_x4` with a properly constructed AES cipher context before calling `_encrypt`.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Invoke any operation that triggers the AES decryptor closure (e.g., decrypt data).
2. Execution reaches the uninitialized pointer call.
3. App crashes or behaves unpredictably.

rules.title: Non-constant-time bitwise operation leaks timing information
rules.description: The function uses data-dependent branches based on secret-derived input (param_1) when computing shifts, leading to variable execution time that can be measured to infer key material.
rules.remediation: Replace conditional branches with constant-time bitwise operations using masks (e.g., via unsigned integer overflow and conditional selection) to ensure uniform execution path.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Identify that the function is used in a cryptographic context (AES S-box/MixColumns).
2. Measure execution time of the operation with different secret-dependent inputs via cache-timing or local profiling.
3. Correlate timing variations with key bits to recover the full key.

rules.title: Uninitialized stack variable returned on error path
rules.description: On error path, the function returns the uninitialized local_30, leaking stack contents which may include sensitive data.
rules.remediation: Initialize local_30 to a safe default (e.g., empty Array) before the encrypt call, or return a proper error result.
rules.pocTemplate:
1. Trigger an error condition during encryption (e.g., malformed input) to make unaff_x21 non-zero.
2. Capture returned Array of UInt8; it will contain uninitialized stack data potentially holding keys or plaintext.
